title: Streaming privilege
summary: Streaming Privilege examines the powerful role that today’s serial television plays in legitimating the ‘new Gilded Age’ of extreme inequality. It is a book about contemporary television series, culture, power, ideology, family and inequality. Through its cultural analysis, the book reveals popular culture’s obsession with wealth, the super-rich and dynastic families. Focusing on four major series – Downton Abbey, The Crown, Succession and Yellowstone – the book explores what today’s most-watched television dramas reveal about contemporary attitudes toward wealth. As dynastic structures once again dominate economy, stories of wealthy families offer a cultural lens through which middle- and working-class audiences make sense of economic disparities. Darwing on the traditions of cultural studies and critical sociology, the book introduces the concepts of family succession drama and luxury television to highlight the role that quality television and its viewing practices play in producing consent to patrimonial forms of capitalism and today’s inheritocracy. The specific interest is in how families, wealth and moral norms intersect in serial television, as this intersection is at the heart of contemporary accumulation processes. The book suggests that much of today’s quality television is politically and morally ambivalent, but that the power of these shows to legitimise inequalities lies precisely in this (metamodernist) ambivalence that reflects today’s perceived societal anomie. Despite their complexities and ambiguities, the four series and other dramas about the rich tend to legitimise, perpetuate and deepen our contemporary inequalities, which are inextricably linked to the socio-economic role of the family.
